questions.q: Complex numbers z₁ and z₂ satisfy |z₁| = 3, |z₂| = 4 and |z₁ + z₂| = 5. What is |z₁ − z₂|?
questions.x: |z₁ + z₂|² + |z₁ − z₂|² = 2(|z₁|² + |z₂|²) = 2(9 + 16) = 50, so |z₁ − z₂|² = 50 − 25 = 25 and |z₁ − z₂| = 5. Check with z₁ = 3, z₂ = 4i: |3 + 4i| = 5 and |3 − 4i| = 5.

questions.q: f(x) = (x − 1)/(x + 2) for x ≠ −2. What is f⁻¹(2)?
questions.x: f⁻¹(2) is the x with f(x) = 2: x − 1 = 2(x + 2), so x = −5. Check: f(−5) = −6/−3 = 2. Computing f(2) = 1/4 instead is the usual slip.

questions.q: Solve log₂x + logₓ2 = 5/2, where x > 0 and x ≠ 1.
questions.x: Put t = log₂x, so logₓ2 = 1/t and t + 1/t = 5/2, i.e. 2t² − 5t + 2 = 0, giving t = 2 or t = ½. Then x = 2² = 4 or x = 2^(1/2) = √2. Check x = √2: ½ + 2 = 5/2.

questions.q: At which points is f(x) = |x − 1| + |x − 2| discontinuous?
questions.x: |x − 1| and |x − 2| are continuous for every real x, so their sum is too. The graph has corners at x = 1 and x = 2, but corners are not breaks: f is continuous everywhere.

questions.q: A = [aᵢⱼ] is a 3 × 3 matrix with |A| = 5, and Aᵢⱼ is the cofactor of aᵢⱼ. What is a₁₁A₂₁ + a₁₂A₂₂ + a₁₃A₂₃?
questions.x: Entries of one row multiplied by the cofactors of a different row always add up to 0: the sum is the expansion of a determinant whose first two rows are equal. The value |A| = 5 comes only from entries and cofactors of the same row.

questions.q: What is the inverse of the matrix [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]?
o: [[cos θ, sin θ], [−sin θ, cos θ]]
questions.x: The determinant is cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, so the inverse is the adjoint: swap the diagonal entries and change the signs of the other two, giving [[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]], which is the transpose.

questions.q: What is the least value of f(x) = x² − 4x + 1 on the interval 3 ≤ x ≤ 5?
questions.x: f(x) = (x − 2)² − 3 has its vertex at x = 2, outside the interval, and f increases for x > 2. So the least value is at x = 3: 9 − 12 + 1 = −2 (and f(5) = 6 is the greatest). Giving the vertex value −3 ignores the interval.

questions.q: ω is a complex cube root of unity. Which of these equals the complex conjugate of ω?
questions.x: The complex cube roots of unity are (−1 + √3 i)/2 and (−1 − √3 i)/2, which are conjugates of each other, and each is the square of the other. So the conjugate of ω is ω². Note 1/ω² = ω, which is ω itself, not its conjugate.

questions.q: What is the sum of the reciprocals of the first 10 terms of the H.P. 1/2, 1/5, 1/8, … ?
questions.x: The reciprocals 2, 5, 8, … form an A.P. with d = 3. Their sum is (10/2)(2 × 2 + 9 × 3) = 5 × 31 = 155. Check: the 10th reciprocal is 29 and 5 × (2 + 29) = 155. Using 10d gives 165.

questions.q: Which term of the A.P. 7, 11, 15, … is 95?
questions.x: aₙ = 7 + (n − 1) × 4 = 95 gives n − 1 = 22, so n = 23. Check: a₂₃ = 7 + 88 = 95. Stopping at n − 1 = 22 gives the 22nd term, which is 91.

questions.q: For 1 ≤ r ≤ n, which expression equals C(n, r)/C(n, r − 1)?
questions.x: C(n, r)/C(n, r − 1) = [n!/(r!(n − r)!)] × [(r − 1)!(n − r + 1)!/n!] = (n − r + 1)/r. Check with n = 5, r = 2: C(5, 2)/C(5, 1) = 10/5 = 2 and (5 − 2 + 1)/2 = 2. The flipped fraction is the most common slip.

questions.q: Which formula for 1³ + 2³ + 3³ + … + n³ can be proved by mathematical induction for every positive integer n?
questions.x: The sum of the first n cubes is the square of 1 + 2 + … + n, that is [n(n + 1)/2]². Test n = 2: 1 + 8 = 9 = 3², while the other formulas give 18, 5 and 6. n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6 is the sum of squares, not cubes.

questions.q: The terminal side of an angle θ (0 ≤ θ < 2π) lies along the line y = −√3x in the second quadrant. What is θ?
questions.x: The point (−1, √3) lies on the line in the second quadrant, so tan θ = −√3 with θ in quadrant II, giving θ = π − π/3 = 2π/3. 5π/3 is the same line in the fourth quadrant.

questions.q: Given cos θ = 1/8 with 0 < θ < π/2, what is sin(θ/2)?
questions.x: sin²(θ/2) = (1 − cos θ)/2 = (7/8)/2 = 7/16, and θ/2 is acute, so sin(θ/2) = √7/4. 3/4 is cos(θ/2), from (1 + cos θ)/2 = 9/16, and 7/16 forgets the square root.

questions.q: The graph of y = A cos(ωx) + D, with A > 0 and ω > 0, has greatest value 7, least value −1 and period 4π. Which function is it?
questions.x: A = (7 − (−1))/2 = 4, D = (7 + (−1))/2 = 3 and 2π/ω = 4π gives ω = 1/2. Taking ω = 2 gives period π, not 4π, and A = 8 uses the full height instead of half of it.

questions.q: A ladder 10 m long leans against a vertical wall, making 60° with the level ground. Its foot slides away from the wall until the angle is 30°. How far down the wall does the top slide?
questions.x: The top is first at 10 sin 60° = 5√3 m and then at 10 sin 30° = 5 m, so it slides 5√3 − 5 = 5(√3 − 1) m. By symmetry the foot moves out by the same amount, 10 cos 30° − 10 cos 60°.

questions.q: What is the area of an equilateral triangle of side 6?
questions.x: Area = ½ × 6 × 6 × sin 60° = 18 × √3/2 = 9√3 (the formula (√3/4)a² gives the same). Leaving out the ½ gives 18√3.

questions.q: The general solution of the pair of equations sin θ = −1/2 and tan θ = 1/√3, holding together, is (n ∈ Z):
questions.x: In one turn sin θ = −1/2 at 7π/6 and 11π/6, and tan θ = 1/√3 at π/6 and 7π/6; only 7π/6 is common. Repeating every 2π gives θ = 2nπ + 7π/6; the form nπ + π/6 also includes π/6, where sin θ = +1/2.

questions.q: If x = y ln y (y > 1), what is dy/dx?
questions.x: dx/dy = ln y + y(1/y) = 1 + ln y, so dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy) = 1/(1 + ln y). Leaving the answer as 1 + ln y gives dx/dy, not dy/dx.

questions.q: What is the derivative of y = 3x⁴ − 2/x, x ≠ 0?
questions.x: d/dx(3x⁴) = 12x³ and −2/x = −2x⁻¹ has derivative 2x⁻² = 2/x². Losing the sign of the power rule on x⁻¹ gives 12x³ − 2/x².

questions.q: If 1/((x − 1)²(x + 1)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)² + C/(x + 1), then A equals:
questions.x: 1 = A(x − 1)(x + 1) + B(x + 1) + C(x − 1)². x = 1 gives B = 1/2, x = −1 gives C = 1/4, and the x² terms give A + C = 0, so A = −1/4. Check x = 0: −A + B + C = 1/4 + 1/2 + 1/4 = 1.

questions.q: The average value of f(x) = x² on the interval [0, 3] is:
questions.x: Average value = (1/(3 − 0))∫₀³ x² dx = (1/3)(27/3) = 3. Forgetting to divide by the length 3 gives 9, and averaging only the end values f(0) and f(3) gives 9/2.

questions.q: Using x = tan θ, ∫ dx/(1 + x²)^(3/2) equals:
questions.x: With x = tan θ, dx = sec²θ dθ and (1 + x²)^(3/2) = sec³θ, so the integral is ∫cos θ dθ = sin θ + C = x/√(1 + x²) + C. Check by differentiating: [(1 + x²) − x²]/(1 + x²)^(3/2).

questions.q: The axes are first translated to the new origin (2, 1) and then rotated through 90°. What are the final coordinates of the point whose original coordinates are (3, 5)?
questions.x: Translation gives (3 − 2, 5 − 1) = (1, 4). Rotating the axes through θ = 90°: X = x cos θ + y sin θ = 4 and Y = −x sin θ + y cos θ = −1, so (4, −1). Rotating the point instead of the axes gives (−4, 1).

questions.q: A triangle has vertices A(1, 2), B(5, 2) and C(3, 6). What is the tangent of its angle at C?
questions.x: Slope of CA = 2 and slope of CB = −2, so tan C = |(2 − (−2))/(1 + 2(−2))| = 4/3; the angle is acute since CA · CB = (−2)(2) + (−4)(−4) = 12 > 0. 2 is tan A, the angle at A.

questions.q: A feasible region has corner points (0, 2), (3, 0), (6, 0), (6, 8) and (0, 5). For z = 4x + 6y, which statement is true?
o: The minimum is 0, at the origin
The minimum 12 occurs at both (0, 2) and (3, 0)
questions.x: At the corners z = 12, 12, 24, 72 and 30. The minimum 12 is reached at two corners (and along the edge 2x + 3y = 6 joining them); the maximum is 72 at (6, 8). The origin is not in the region.

questions.q: An ellipse has foci (1, 0) and (5, 0), and its major axis has length 6. What is its equation?
questions.x: Centre = midpoint (3, 0), c = 2 and a = 3, so b² = 9 − 4 = 5: (x − 3)²/9 + y²/5 = 1. Check: the vertex (6, 0) is 5 and 1 from the foci, total 6.

questions.q: What is the shortest distance from the point (7, 4) to the circle x² + y² − 2x − 4y − 11 = 0?
questions.x: Centre (1, 2), radius √(1 + 4 + 11) = 4. The point is √(36 + 4) = 2√10 from the centre, outside the circle, so the shortest distance is 2√10 − 4. 2√6 is the length of the tangent.

questions.q: The parallelogram with adjacent sides i + j and λi + 2j has area 3. What are the possible values of λ?
questions.x: (i + j) × (λi + 2j) = (2 − λ)k, so |2 − λ| = 3, giving λ = −1 or λ = 5. Keeping only one sign of the absolute value loses a solution.

questions.q: Particles P and Q leave the origin together at t = 0 along the same line. P has velocity 2t m/s and Q a constant velocity 4 m/s. How far from the origin are they when they next meet?
questions.x: P's displacement is t² and Q's is 4t. They meet when t² = 4t, i.e. t = 4 s, at 16 m. At t = 2 s their velocities are equal, but P is at 4 m and Q at 8 m.

questions.q: The speed v of a wave on a stretched string depends only on the tension F and the mass per unit length μ of the string. Dimensional analysis gives:
questions.x: Let v = kFᵃμᵇ: [LT⁻¹] = [MLT⁻²]ᵃ[ML⁻¹]ᵇ. T: −2a = −1, so a = ½; M: a + b = 0, so b = −½; L check: a − b = 1. So v ∝ √(F/μ). Swapping the signs of the powers gives √(μ/F).

questions.q: A force of 50 N acts at a point 0.5 m from a pivot. The force makes 30° with the line joining the pivot to that point (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = √3/2). The moment arm of the force about the pivot is:
questions.x: Moment arm = perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action = r sin θ = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 m. Using cos 30° gives 0.25√3 m; taking the whole 0.5 m ignores the angle.

questions.q: A car travels 30 km due east in 0.5 h and then 10 km due west in the next 0.5 h. Its average velocity for the whole trip is:
questions.x: Net displacement = 30 − 10 = 20 km due east in a total of 1 h, so average velocity = 20 km h⁻¹ due east. Using the total distance 40 km gives the average speed, 40 km h⁻¹, not the velocity.

questions.q: The area between a velocity–time graph and the time axis gives the body's:
questions.x: Area = velocity × time, which has the unit of length, so it gives the displacement. The slope of the same graph gives the acceleration, the usual mix-up.

questions.q: A constant upward force of 30 N lifts a 2 kg mass vertically through 5 m. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the net work done on the mass by all the forces is:
questions.x: Work by the 30 N force = 30 × 5 = 150 J; work by gravity = −20 × 5 = −100 J; net work = 50 J, which equals the mass's gain in kinetic energy. 150 J is the work of the applied force alone.

questions.q: A planet has the same average density as the Earth but twice the Earth's radius. If the escape velocity from the Earth is v, the escape velocity from the planet is:
questions.x: With the same density, M ∝ R³, so M/R ∝ R² and v = √(2GM/R) ∝ R; twice the radius gives 2v. Check: mass 8 times, radius 2 times, √(8/2) = 2. Forgetting that the mass also grows gives √2 v or a smaller value.

questions.q: A turntable starts from rest with a uniform angular acceleration of 4π rad s⁻². How many revolutions does it make in the first 5 s?
questions.x: θ = ½αt² = ½ × 4π × 25 = 50π rad, and one revolution is 2π rad, so it makes 50π/2π = 25 revolutions. Forgetting the ½ gives 50.

questions.q: Two boats moving fast side by side, close together and parallel, tend to be pulled towards each other. The reason is that:
o: Water flows slower between them, so the pressure there is lower than on their outer sides
Water flows faster between them, so the pressure there is lower than on their outer sides
The boats attract each other by gravitation
The waves from each boat push the other boat towards it
questions.x: The water squeezed through the narrow gap moves faster, and by Bernoulli's principle faster flow means lower pressure. The higher pressure on the outer sides pushes the boats together. Gravitational attraction between boats is far too small to matter.

questions.q: The length of a simple pendulum is increased by 44%. Its time period increases by:
questions.x: T ∝ √l, so the new period is √1.44 = 1.2 times the old one: an increase of 20%. Taking T ∝ l gives 44%; halving 44% (the small-change approximation used for a large change) gives 22%.

questions.q: Two coherent waves interfere. At points of complete destructive interference there is no energy. This is because the energy is:
o: Converted into heat at the minima
Redistributed, being greater at the maxima, so the total is conserved
Reflected back to the sources from the minima
questions.x: Interference does not create or destroy energy: the intensity is zero at the minima and four times that of one wave at the maxima, so the energy is only redistributed and the total is unchanged.

questions.q: An electric bell rings inside a glass jar. As the air is pumped out, the sound heard gets fainter, although the bell is still seen to vibrate. This shows that:
o: Glass does not let sound through
Sound needs a material medium to travel
Sound travels faster in a vacuum
questions.x: The bell is still vibrating, but with less and less air to carry the vibrations less sound reaches us: sound needs a medium. The sound was heard through the glass at first, so glass does transmit sound.

questions.q: According to Huygens' principle, every point on a wavefront:
o: Stays at rest while the wavefront moves on
Sends out wavelets only backwards, towards the source
Acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out with the speed of the wave
Sends out wavelets that travel faster than the wave itself
questions.x: Huygens' principle treats each point of a wavefront as a new source of secondary wavelets moving forward at the wave speed; the new wavefront is the surface touching them all. The wavelets do not move faster than the wave.

questions.q: An object is placed 1.1 cm from the objective of a compound microscope, whose focal length is 1 cm. What linear magnification does the objective produce?
questions.x: 1/q = 1/f − 1/p = 1 − 1/1.1 = 0.1/1.1, so q = 11 cm and m = q/p = 11/1.1 = 10. Check: the object is 0.1 cm beyond the focus, and m = f/0.1 = 10. Taking the image distance itself as the magnification gives 11.

questions.q: 200 J of work is done on a gas while it gives out 50 J of heat to its surroundings. The change in the internal energy of the gas is:
questions.x: Energy gained = work done on the gas − heat lost = 200 − 50 = +150 J. Treating the heat lost as heat gained gives 250 J.

questions.q: An ideal gas with Cp = 3.5R is heated at constant pressure and absorbs 700 J of heat. How much work does the gas do?
questions.x: Q = nCpΔT = 3.5nRΔT, and the work at constant pressure is W = pΔV = nRΔT = 700/3.5 = 200 J. Check: ΔU = nCvΔT = 2.5 × 200 = 500 J, and 500 + 200 = 700 J. 500 J is the rise in internal energy, not the work.

questions.q: Filling the space between the plates of a capacitor with a dielectric increases its capacitance because the dielectric:
o: Conducts charge from one plate to the other
Increases the charge on the plates by itself
Becomes polarised, which reduces the field and the potential difference for the same charge
questions.x: The induced surface charges of the polarised dielectric oppose the field of the plates, so for the same Q the field and V are smaller; C = Q/V therefore increases by the factor εr. A dielectric is an insulator.

questions.q: In Millikan's experiment an oil drop is held at rest between horizontal plates. The potential difference across the plates is then suddenly doubled. Just after the change, the drop:
questions.x: At rest qE = mg. Doubling V doubles E, so the upward force becomes 2mg; the net force is 2mg − mg = mg upward, giving an upward acceleration g (before air drag builds up).

questions.q: A heater takes power P from a fixed-voltage supply. Its coil is cut in half and only one half is connected to the same supply. Assuming the resistance does not change with temperature, the power taken is now:
questions.x: Half the coil has resistance R/2, and P = V²/R with V fixed, so the power doubles to 2P. Using P = I²R with the old current gives P/2.

questions.q: In a Wheatstone bridge, P and Q are in series in one branch and R and S in series in the other, both branches across a battery; a galvanometer joins the P–Q junction to the R–S junction. The bridge is balanced. If the battery and the galvanometer are interchanged, the galvanometer:
o: Shows a deflection that depends on the battery's emf
questions.x: The balance condition P/Q = R/S can be rewritten P/R = Q/S, which is exactly the balance condition with the battery and galvanometer swapped. So the bridge stays balanced.

questions.q: The SI unit of the permeability of free space, μ₀, can be written as:
questions.x: From B = μ₀I/(2πr), μ₀ = 2πrB/I, so its unit is T × m / A = T m A⁻¹, matching μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.

questions.q: A current changing at 5 A s⁻¹ in coil P induces an emf of 2 V in a nearby coil Q. If instead the current in Q changes at 5 A s⁻¹, with the coils in the same positions, the emf induced in P is:
questions.x: The mutual inductance of a pair of coils is the same either way: M = 2/5 = 0.4 H. So the same rate of change in Q induces 0.4 × 5 = 2 V in P. 0.4 is the value of M in henry, not the emf.

questions.q: An AC generator has a peak emf of 200 V. Its coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. At the instant the plane of the coil makes an angle of 60° with the field direction, the instantaneous emf is (sin 60° ≈ 0.87, cos 60° = 0.5):
questions.x: The emf is greatest when the plane is parallel to the field and zero when it is perpendicular, so ε = ε₀ cos(angle between plane and field) = 200 × cos 60° = 100 V. (Equivalently, the normal is at 30° to B and ε = ε₀ sin 30°.) Using sin 60° gives 174 V.

questions.q: The speed of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum is related to the permeability μ₀ and permittivity ε₀ of free space by:
questions.x: Maxwell's theory gives c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀); with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹ this is about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. 1/(μ₀ε₀) is c², not c.

questions.q: Pure silicon has a forbidden energy gap of about 1.1 eV. Very close to 0 K, pure silicon behaves as:
o: A good conductor, because its resistance falls as the temperature falls
An insulator, because no electrons have enough energy to cross into the conduction band
questions.x: At 0 K there is no thermal energy to lift electrons across the 1.1 eV gap, so the valence band is full, the conduction band is empty and no current can flow: silicon is an insulator. Falling resistance with falling temperature is metallic behaviour; a semiconductor's resistance rises as it is cooled.

questions.q: A good p-n junction diode is tested with an ohmmeter, first with the leads one way round and then reversed. The two readings should be:
o: A low resistance one way and a very high resistance the other way
questions.x: Forward biased, the junction has a low resistance; reverse biased, it has a very high resistance. Low both ways means a short-circuited diode, and very high both ways means an open-circuited one.

questions.q: An electron and a proton are each confined to the same region of width Δx. The proton's mass is 1836 times the electron's. Using Δx Δp ≈ h, the ratio (uncertainty in the electron's speed)/(uncertainty in the proton's speed) is about:
questions.x: Both have the same Δp ≈ h/Δx, and Δv = Δp/m, so Δv is inversely proportional to the mass: Δv_e/Δv_p = m_p/m_e = 1836. Inverting the ratio gives 1/1836; equal Δp does not mean equal Δv.

questions.q: A beam of light falls on a photocell connected in a circuit with a relay. A burglar alarm rings when a person walks through the beam because:
o: Blocking the light increases the photoelectric current
Blocking the light stops the photoelectric current in the photocell
The light changes its frequency when blocked
questions.x: While light falls on the cathode, photoelectrons give a current that holds the relay; when the beam is cut, emission and the current stop, and the relay switches on the alarm. The person does not change the light's frequency.

questions.q: According to Bohr's postulate, an electron can move only in those orbits for which its angular momentum mvr is equal to:
questions.x: Bohr's quantisation condition is mvr = nh/2π, an integral multiple of h/2π. nhf is Planck's energy of quanta, and h/(mv) is the de Broglie wavelength, not an angular momentum.

questions.q: On the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number, for nuclei heavier than iron-56 the binding energy per nucleon:
o: Increases steadily as the mass number increases
Decreases slowly as the mass number increases
Is the same for every nucleus
questions.x: After its peak of about 8.8 MeV near iron-56, the curve falls slowly, to about 7.6 MeV for uranium-238, because the growing proton-proton repulsion makes large nuclei less tightly bound. A steady rise describes only the light nuclei.

questions.q: Ultrasound used in medical scanning is sound with a frequency:
o: Below 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear
Above 20 kHz, too high for humans to hear
Equal to that of visible light
questions.x: Ultrasound means sound above the upper limit of human hearing, about 20 kHz; medical scanners use a few MHz. Below 20 Hz is infrasound, and sound is a mechanical wave, not light.

questions.q: 11.2 g of iron is heated with 8.0 g of sulphur, Fe + S → FeS, and 13.2 g of FeS is obtained. The percentage yield is: (S = 32, Fe = 56)
questions.x: Fe = 0.2 mol and S = 0.25 mol; they react 1 : 1, so Fe is limiting. Theoretical FeS = 0.2 × 88 = 17.6 g; yield = 13.2/17.6 × 100 = 75%. Using sulphur as limiting gives 22 g and 60%; comparing with the total mass of reactants (19.2 g) gives about 69%.

questions.q: In paper chromatography, the stationary phase is:
o: The solvent that rises up the paper
Water held in the cellulose fibres of the paper
The mixture applied as a spot
The vapour of the solvent in the jar
questions.x: The paper's fibres hold a film of water, which is the stationary phase; the solvent moving up the paper is the mobile phase. Mixing up the stationary and mobile phases is the usual slip.

questions.q: For a gas, the van der Waals constant a = 4.0 atm dm⁶ mol⁻². For 2 mol of this gas in a 4 dm³ vessel, the pressure correction term an²/V² is:
questions.x: an²/V² = 4.0 × 2²/4² = 4.0 × 4/16 = 1.0 atm. Forgetting to square n and V (4.0 × 2/4) gives 2.0 atm.

questions.q: How much heat is needed to change 18 g of ice at 0 °C into steam at 100 °C? (Enthalpy of fusion of ice = 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹; enthalpy of vaporisation of water = 40.7 kJ mol⁻¹; specific heat of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹; H = 1, O = 16)
questions.x: 18 g is 1 mol. Melting: 6.0 kJ. Heating water 0 → 100 °C: 18 × 4.2 × 100 = 7560 J = 7.56 kJ. Boiling: 40.7 kJ. Total = 54.26 ≈ 54.3 kJ. Leaving out the heating step gives 46.7 kJ, and leaving out melting gives 48.3 kJ.

questions.q: An object placed in the path of cathode rays casts a sharp shadow on the end of the discharge tube. This shows that cathode rays:
o: Are deflected by a magnetic field
questions.x: A sharp shadow forms only if the rays travel in straight lines from the cathode. Their negative charge and mass are shown by other experiments (deflection by fields, turning a paddle wheel).

questions.q: According to VSEPR theory, how are the four electron pairs around the oxygen atom in a water molecule arranged, and what is the shape of the molecule?
questions.x: Oxygen has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, which point roughly to the corners of a tetrahedron. The shape names only the positions of the atoms, so with two corners taken by lone pairs the molecule is bent. Calling the molecule tetrahedral confuses the arrangement of electron pairs with the shape.

questions.q: In molecular orbital theory, the bond order of a diatomic molecule is equal to:
o: The total number of electrons in bonding orbitals
The difference between the numbers of bonding and antibonding orbitals
Half the total number of valence electrons
Half the difference between the numbers of electrons in bonding and antibonding orbitals
questions.x: Bond order = ½(bonding electrons − antibonding electrons); for H₂ it is ½(2 − 0) = 1. Forgetting the factor of one half doubles every bond order, the usual slip.

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine?
questions.x: Enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change to form one mole of gaseous atoms from the element in its standard state, so half a mole of Cl₂ gives one mole of Cl(g). Cl₂ → 2Cl is the bond energy of Cl₂, which forms two moles of atoms, the most tempting slip.

questions.q: For a reversible reaction at equilibrium, which quantity is zero?
o: The rate of the forward reaction
The rate constant of the reverse reaction
questions.x: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so the net rate (forward minus reverse) is zero. Saying the forward rate is zero describes a reaction that has stopped, which is the static picture of equilibrium.

questions.q: In qualitative analysis, NH₄Cl is added before NH₄OH to precipitate Fe³⁺ and Al³⁺ as hydroxides. The NH₄Cl is added because:
o: It reacts with Fe³⁺ and Al³⁺ to form insoluble chlorides
It raises [OH⁻] so that all metal hydroxides precipitate
It acts as a catalyst for the precipitation
Its NH₄⁺ ions suppress the ionisation of NH₄OH, keeping [OH⁻] low so that only hydroxides with very small Ksp precipitate
questions.x: NH₄⁺ is common to NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, so the equilibrium shifts left and [OH⁻] stays small. Then the ionic product exceeds Ksp only for hydroxides with very low Ksp, such as Fe(OH)₃ and Al(OH)₃, while hydroxides like Mg(OH)₂ stay in solution. FeCl₃ and AlCl₃ are soluble, so the chloride option is wrong.

questions.q: Dissolving 10 g of a non-volatile non-electrolyte in 180 g of water lowers the vapour pressure of the water by 1.0% at a given temperature. Approximately what is the molar mass of the solute?
questions.x: Relative lowering = mole fraction of solute ≈ n(solute)/n(water) = 0.010. n(water) = 180/18 = 10 mol, so n(solute) ≈ 0.10 mol and M ≈ 10/0.10 = 100 g mol⁻¹. Reading 1.0% as 0.10 instead of 0.010 gives 10 g mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride is electrolysed using carbon electrodes. What are the main products?
o: Copper at the cathode, chlorine at the anode
Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode
Copper at the cathode, oxygen at the anode
Chlorine at the cathode, copper at the anode
questions.x: Cu²⁺ is reduced more easily than water, so copper deposits on the cathode. At the anode, concentrated Cl⁻ is discharged as chlorine. Hydrogen would form only for a metal above hydrogen in the series, such as sodium.

questions.q: Faraday's first law of electrolysis states that the mass of a substance deposited or set free at an electrode is:
o: Directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed
Inversely proportional to the quantity of electricity passed
Independent of the time for which the current flows
Directly proportional to the square of the current
questions.x: m ∝ Q, where Q = I × t. So the mass doubles if the current or the time doubles; it does not depend on the square of the current.

questions.q: In a reaction in solution, neutral molecules react to form ions and no gas is given off. Which physical measurement is most suitable for following the rate of this reaction?
o: Loss in mass of the flask
questions.x: As ions form, the solution conducts better, so conductivity changes in step with the extent of reaction. Gas volume, loss of mass and pressure all need a gas to be given off, which this reaction does not do.

questions.q: Aluminium oxide is amphoteric. 10.2 g of Al₂O₃ dissolves completely in aqueous NaOH to form sodium aluminate, which contains one sodium for each aluminium. What mass of NaOH is used? (Al = 27, O = 16, Na = 23, H = 1)
questions.x: Al₂O₃ = 102 g mol⁻¹, so 10.2 g = 0.10 mol, containing 0.20 mol Al. One Na per Al needs 0.20 mol NaOH = 8.0 g (Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄]). Taking 1 NaOH per Al₂O₃ gives 4.0 g; the 1 : 6 ratio for HCl would give 24.0 g.

questions.q: A solution of beryllium chloride in water is acidic. The best explanation is that:
o: Be²⁺ ions combine with OH⁻ ions taken from the air
The small, highly polarising Be²⁺ ion pulls electron density from its bound water molecules, so [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺ releases H⁺
Chloride ions react with water to give HCl and OH⁻
Beryllium chloride is oxidised by water to give chlorine
questions.x: Be²⁺ is tiny and doubly charged, so it strongly polarises the O–H bonds of the water molecules bound to it: [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺ + H₂O ⇌ [Be(H₂O)₃(OH)]⁺ + H₃O⁺. Cl⁻ is the ion of a strong acid and does not hydrolyse, so the chloride option is wrong.

questions.q: White phosphorus is warmed with NaOH solution: P₄ + 3NaOH + 3H₂O → PH₃ + 3NaH₂PO₂. This reaction is best described as, with the oxidation states of phosphorus formed:
questions.x: Phosphorus starts at 0; in PH₃ it is −3 and in H₂PO₂⁻ it is +1 (2(+1) + x + 2(−2) = −1). One element is both reduced and oxidised, so it is disproportionation; electron check: 1 P gains 3 e⁻ while 3 P lose 1 e⁻ each. Assuming the oxyanion is phosphite (+3) is the tempting slip.

questions.q: Plastic (amorphous) sulphur is obtained by:
o: Cooling a solution of sulphur in carbon disulphide slowly
Melting rhombic sulphur and letting it cool slowly in a crucible
Pouring nearly boiling sulphur into cold water
questions.x: Sudden cooling of hot, viscous sulphur (long chains) in cold water traps the chains and gives rubbery plastic sulphur. Slow crystallisation from CS₂ gives rhombic sulphur and slow cooling of the melt gives monoclinic needles.

questions.q: In titrations with KMnO₄, the solution is acidified with dilute H₂SO₄ and not with dilute HCl because:
o: KMnO₄ would oxidise HCl to chlorine, using up extra permanganate
HCl would reduce the purple colour of KMnO₄ to green MnO₄²⁻
H₂SO₄ is a stronger oxidising agent than KMnO₄
HCl would precipitate manganese as MnCl₂
questions.x: MnO₄⁻ is strong enough to oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂, so with HCl part of the permanganate is wasted and the titre is too high; sulphate is not oxidised. MnCl₂ is soluble, so the precipitation option is wrong.

questions.q: Heterolytic fission of a covalent bond is favoured when:
o: The bond is non-polar and the reaction is in sunlight
The reaction is in the gas phase at very high temperature
The bond is polar and the reaction is in a polar solvent
questions.x: Heterolysis gives ions, which are stabilised by a polar solvent, and it occurs most easily when the bond is already polar, such as C–Br. Light, high temperature in the gas phase and peroxides favour homolysis into free radicals.

questions.q: Which species is a nucleophile?
questions.x: A nucleophile donates an electron pair; NH₃ has a lone pair on nitrogen. BF₃, NO₂⁺ and CH₃⁺ are electron-deficient electron-pair acceptors, i.e. electrophiles.

questions.q: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃, is chlorinated in sunlight. Only 2 of its 8 hydrogen atoms are on the middle carbon, yet 2-chloropropane forms in about the same amount as 1-chloropropane. The best reason is that:
o: Primary hydrogen atoms are more numerous, so they react faster
Cl⁺ ions attack the carbon atom that carries the most electrons
The secondary C–H bond breaks more easily, giving the more stable secondary free radical
questions.x: A Cl• removes a hydrogen; (CH₃)₂CH• (secondary) is more stable than CH₃CH₂CH₂• (primary), so each secondary H reacts several times faster than a primary H. Counting H atoms alone would predict 3:1 for 1-chloropropane; the reaction is free-radical, not ionic.

questions.q: How many isomers of molecular formula C₈H₁₀ contain a benzene ring?
questions.x: Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, plus three dimethylbenzenes (1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-). Answering 3 counts only the dimethylbenzenes and forgets ethylbenzene.

questions.q: The rate of SN2 reactions falls in the order CH₃Br > CH₃CH₂Br > (CH₃)₂CHBr > (CH₃)₃CBr. The main reason is that:
o: Alkyl groups crowd the back of the carbon atom and hinder the approach of the nucleophile
Tertiary carbocations are less stable than methyl carbocations
The C–Br bond is much stronger in tertiary bromides
Tertiary bromides are more polar than bromomethane
questions.x: In SN2 the nucleophile must reach the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group; each extra alkyl group blocks this path. Carbocation stability belongs to SN1 and actually runs the other way (tertiary most stable).

questions.q: Propan-1-ol is heated under reflux with excess acidified potassium dichromate(VI). The final organic product is:
questions.x: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to the aldehyde; under reflux with excess oxidant the propanal cannot escape and is oxidised further to CH₃CH₂COOH. Propanal is obtained only if it is distilled off as it forms; propanone comes from propan-2-ol.

questions.q: In the Cannizzaro reaction 2HCHO + NaOH → CH₃OH + HCOONa, the oxidation number of carbon changes from:
questions.x: HCHO: 2(+1) + C + (−2) = 0, so C = 0. CH₃OH: 4(+1) + C + (−2) = 0, C = −2. HCOO⁻: (+1) + C + 2(−2) = −1, C = +2. One molecule is reduced and one oxidised (disproportionation); swapping the two is the common slip.

questions.q: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with methylamine, CH₃NH₂, to give compound P. P is then boiled with aqueous NaOH. The products of this second step are:
questions.x: CH₃COCl + CH₃NH₂ → CH₃CONHCH₃ (N-methylethanamide) + HCl. Alkaline hydrolysis of this amide gives CH₃COONa and free CH₃NH₂. Ethanoic acid with methylammonium chloride would come from acid hydrolysis; splitting the molecule at the wrong carbon gives the methanoate/ethylamine pair.

questions.q: Glyceryl trioleate (884 g mol⁻¹) is a triglyceride in which each of the three fatty acid chains contains one C=C bond. What mass of hydrogen is needed to saturate 88.4 g of it completely? (H₂ = 2 g mol⁻¹)
questions.x: 88.4/884 = 0.10 mol of fat; each molecule has three C=C bonds, so 0.30 mol H₂ = 0.30 × 2 = 0.6 g. Allowing only one C=C per molecule gives 0.2 g; using moles of H atoms instead of H₂ gives 0.3 g.

questions.q: In the mass spectrum of butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, a peak appears at m/z = 29. It is due to the ion:
questions.x: Breaking the central C–C bond gives CH₃CH₂⁺, with mass 2 × 12 + 5 = 29. CH₃⁺ is at 15, C₃H₇⁺ at 43 and the molecular ion C₄H₁₀⁺ at 58.

questions.q: When chlorine is added to drinking water, the species mainly responsible for killing bacteria is:
questions.x: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl; chloric(I) acid, HOCl, is the strong disinfecting oxidant. HCl and Cl⁻ have no germ-killing power, though HCl forms in the same reaction, which makes it tempting.

questions.q: Using 8-bit 2's complement, how is the decimal number −5 written?
questions.x: +5 is 00000101; inverting every bit gives 11111010 (the 1's complement), and adding 1 gives 11111011. 10000101 is the sign-and-magnitude form, not 2's complement.

questions.q: A printed page is scanned, and the computer then turns the picture of the text into characters that can be edited in a word processor. Which technology does this?
questions.x: OCR software recognises the shapes of letters in a scanned image and converts them into editable text. OMR only detects marks in set places, such as filled circles, and cannot read ordinary printed words.

questions.q: A quad-core processor has:
o: Four times as much RAM as normal
Four processing cores on one chip
questions.x: "Quad" means four: a quad-core processor has four cores, each able to execute instructions, in a single processor package. The number of cores says nothing about disks or RAM.

questions.q: To return later to a useful web page without remembering or retyping its address, you can save it in the browser as a:
questions.x: A bookmark (called a favourite in some browsers) stores a page's address so it can be opened again with one click. A cookie is a small file a website stores to remember the user, not something the user saves to revisit a page.

questions.q: A full mesh network has 6 computers. A seventh computer is added and the network is kept a full mesh. How many new links are needed?
questions.x: The new computer must have its own link to each of the 6 existing computers, so 6 links are added (the total goes from 15 to 21). 21 is the new total, not the number of new links.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is closest to the user and is where protocols such as HTTP and FTP work for programs like browsers?
questions.x: The Application layer is the top layer (layer 7), giving network services to user programs through protocols such as HTTP, FTP and SMTP. The Physical layer is at the bottom, dealing with raw bits on the medium.

questions.q: Small text files that a website stores on a user's computer to remember her visits and settings, and which can also be used to track her browsing, are called:
questions.x: Cookies are small files saved by websites; they are useful for settings but raise privacy concerns because they can track a user across visits. They are not programs that spread like viruses.

questions.q: To handle more visitors, a website adds more servers so that the load is shared among them. This is called:
questions.x: Adding more machines to share the work is scaling out, or horizontal scaling. Scaling up means making one existing server more powerful, for example by giving it more memory.

questions.q: A bank card that takes the money straight from the holder's own bank account at the time of payment is a:
questions.x: A debit card draws on money already in the holder's account. A credit card lets the holder pay later, as a short loan from the bank.

questions.q: An operating system that must respond to events within a fixed, guaranteed short time, as in a system that controls an aircraft's engines, is a:
questions.x: A real-time OS guarantees a response within strict time limits, which control systems need. A batch OS runs collected jobs later with no quick response.

questions.q: Cell A7 holds `=SUM(A1:A5)`. A new row is then inserted above row 3. Which formula does the total cell (now A8) contain?
questions.x: The new row falls inside A1:A5, so the range grows to include it: A1 and A2 stay, and the old rows 3 to 5 move down to 4 to 6, giving `=SUM(A1:A6)`. Keeping A1:A5 would leave out the last value, now in A6.

questions.q: An indexed sequential file has this index, each entry giving the lowest key in a block: 100 → block 1, 250 → block 2, 400 → block 3, 550 → block 4. Records are stored in key order. In which block is the record with key 390?
questions.x: Block 2 holds the keys from 250 up to just below 400, and 250 ≤ 390 < 400, so the record is in block 2. Block 3 starts at key 400, which is already larger than 390.

questions.q: Each country has exactly one capital city, and each capital city is the capital of one country. What type of relationship is Country–Capital?
questions.x: One instance on each side is linked to exactly one instance on the other side, so the relationship is one-to-one. One-to-many would need a country with several capitals.

questions.q: In the functional dependency RollNo → Name, what is RollNo called?
questions.x: The attribute on the left of the arrow determines the one on the right, so RollNo is the determinant and Name is the dependent attribute.

questions.q:
Table Book(BookID, Title, Subject, Price) holds these rows: (1, Algebra, Maths, 450), (2, Optics, Physics, 600), (3, Calculus, Maths, 700), (4, Atoms, Chemistry, 350), (5, Mechanics, Physics, 500), (6, Geometry, Maths, 400).
How many rows does this query return?
```
SELECT DISTINCT Subject FROM Book;
```
questions.x: DISTINCT removes repeated values, leaving Maths, Physics and Chemistry: 3 rows. Without DISTINCT one row per book, 6 rows, would be shown.
An integer constant that starts with 0 is octal, so 012 = 1 × 8 + 2 = 10, and x + 1 = 11 in decimal. Reading 012 as decimal twelve gives 13.

questions.q: A program has been compiled and linked into an executable file. The source file is then deleted. What happens when the executable file is run?
o: It fails, because the source file is read each time it runs
It runs normally, since it no longer needs the source file
It runs only after the program is compiled again
It shows the source code instead of running
questions.x: The executable already contains the machine code, so the source file is not needed to run it. The source is needed only to change and recompile the program.

questions.q: A source file has three `#include` lines and one `#define` line. After preprocessing, how many of these four lines are still present, unchanged, in the code passed to the compiler?
questions.x: The preprocessor replaces each #include line with the header's contents and uses the #define line to replace the macro name, then drops it. So none of the four directive lines reach the compiler as written.
Control jumps to case 2 and adds 20; with no break it falls through into case 1 and adds 10, so s = 30. case 3 is above the entry point, so its 30 is never added (60 would add all three).
op holds '-', so control jumps to case '-' and prints 12 - 4 = 8; break then leaves the switch. default runs only when no case matches.
s grows 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 while i goes 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Now s < 15 is false, so the loop stops with i = 6 and s = 15. i was already increased after the last addition, so 5 15 is wrong.

questions.q: During a feasibility study, a team compares the expected cost of building a new system with the money the system will save over the next few years. Which kind of feasibility is this?
questions.x: Economic (financial) feasibility asks whether the benefits are worth the cost. Technical feasibility asks whether the hardware, software and skills are available, not whether it pays.

questions.q: Agile methods value which of these more than comprehensive documentation?
o: Formal sign-off at the end of each stage
questions.x: Agile puts working software ahead of heavy documentation, and also values customer collaboration over contract negotiation and responding to change over following a plan. So contracts, fixed plans and stage sign-offs are the things Agile values less, not more.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
s = "KARACHI"
for i in range(0, len(s), 3):
    print(s[i], end="")
```
questions.x: len(s) is 7, so i takes 0, 3, 6; s[0] is 'K', s[3] is 'A' and s[6] is 'I', printed together: KAI. KRCI would be a step of 2.

questions.q: Which built-in Python function tells you the data type of a value, for example whether it is an `int` or a `str`?
questions.x: `type(x)` returns the class of `x`, such as <class 'int'>. `len()` gives a length and `str()` converts a value to text; neither reports the type.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
count = 0
def inc():
    global count
    count += 2
inc()
inc()
print(count)
```
questions.x: `global count` makes the function change the variable outside it, so the two calls add 2 twice: 4. Without `global` the line `count += 2` would raise an error, not print 0.

questions.q: Which is the best description of an algorithm?
o: A program written in a high-level language
A finite sequence of clear steps that solves a problem
A diagram of the parts of a computer
Any list of steps, even one that never ends
questions.x: An algorithm is a finite, well-defined set of steps for solving a problem, and it can be written in any form, not only as a program. A list of steps that never ends fails finiteness.

questions.q: In a tree, R is the root with children S and T; S has children U and V; V has one child, W. How many leaf nodes does the tree have?
questions.x: A leaf has no children: U, W and T are leaves, so 3. V is not a leaf because it has the child W; counting V gives the wrong answer 4.

questions.q: Marks: 6, 9, 3, 9, 8. What are the mean, median and mode, in that order?
questions.x: Mean = 35 / 5 = 7. Sorted: 3, 6, 8, 9, 9, so the median is 8; 9 occurs twice, so the mode is 9. 3 is the middle value before sorting, not the median.

questions.q: A team writes down as many ideas as possible for an app that helps students share notes, without judging any idea yet. Which design thinking stage is this?
questions.x: Generating many possible solutions freely is the Ideate stage. Prototype comes next, when a chosen idea is turned into a simple model.

questions.q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: why city shops charge too much for shawls
the history of shawl weaving in villages
how weavers can gain a fairer share of what their work earns
why traders should be driven out of weaving villages
questions.x: The passage describes the weaver's small share and argues that cooperatives can pay her "something close to what their work is worth". Driving out traders is rejected: without a replacement "she would be worse off".

questions.q: According to the passage, why does the weaver depend on the trader?
o: He pays her more than city shops would
He gives her yarn and buyers she cannot reach on her own
He owns the loom she works on
He trains her to weave new designs
questions.x: She "has no other way to buy yarn in bulk, no means of reaching distant buyers and no savings to wait". He does not pay more than shops: the shop price is "several times as much".

questions.q: The writer would most likely agree that simply driving traders out of weaving villages would:
o: make the weavers rich at once
harm the weavers unless something else took over the trader's role
make no difference to the weavers' earnings
force city shops to lower their prices
questions.x: "Take away the trader without replacing what he provides, and she would be worse off", and the cooperative is the replacement the writer proposes. Nothing suggests they would grow rich at once; the writer says the opposite.

questions.q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "symptom" most nearly means:
o: a feeling of illness in the body
a sign of a deeper problem rather than its cause
the main cause of a difficulty
a dishonest person who cheats others
questions.x: The trader is "a symptom more than a cause": he exists because of the weaver's deeper lack of yarn, buyers and savings. "The main cause" is the opposite of what the sentence says.

questions.q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards weavers' cooperatives?
o: Hopeful but realistic about how hard they are to run
Doubtful that any of them can ever succeed
Dismissive, regarding them as a form of charity
questions.x: The writer calls them "The more useful answer" but admits they need "patience, honest bookkeeping" and "many fail". Charity is ruled out by the words "not charity".

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
o: Delayed soreness comes from small injuries that the body repairs and learns to resist
Muscle soreness shows that a person has exercised in the wrong way
Acid left in the muscles causes pain that lasts for several days
Downhill running should be avoided by all beginners
questions.x: The passage traces the ache to "tiny tears in muscle fibres" and says it is "mostly a sign of adaptation". The acid idea is the one the passage rejects: it "does not fit the timing".

questions.q: According to the passage, which kind of movement causes the most damage to muscle fibres?
o: One done very quickly with no load at all
One in which the muscle holds a weight without moving
One repeated many times on level ground
One in which the muscle lengthens as it works
questions.x: "The damage is greatest in movements where a muscle lengthens while it works, such as lowering a heavy load". Holding a weight still is not mentioned.

questions.q: The passage suggests that walking down a steep hill is likely to cause more soreness than walking up it because:
o: going down produces more acid in the muscles
walking uphill tears more of the muscle fibres
going down makes the leg muscles lengthen while they work
going down is faster and so tires the heart
questions.x: Walking downhill is given as an example of a muscle that "lengthens while it works", the movement that does the most damage. Acid is wrong because the passage says acid does not cause the ache at all.

questions.q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "ordeal" most nearly means:
questions.x: When soreness arrives, "climbing stairs becomes an ordeal" and sitting is "a careful, groaning business", so the word means a painful, hard experience. Nothing in it is exciting.

questions.q: What is the main function of the second paragraph?
o: It describes how soreness can be prevented by gradual training
It lists the symptoms that soreness produces
It rejects a common explanation and offers a better-supported one
It defends the belief that acid causes soreness
questions.x: It opens "That explanation does not fit the timing" and then gives the view that soreness comes "from tiny tears in muscle fibres". Gradual training is the advice of the third paragraph.
